(CNN)  -- A suburban Philadelphia swim club has invited children from a largely minority day-care center to come back after a June reversal that fueled allegations of racism against the club, a spokeswoman said Sunday. Some kids from the Creative Steps Day Care center say club members made racial remarks. The development came during a hastily called Sunday afternoon meeting of the Valley Club in Huntingdon Valley, Pennsylvania. Club members voted overwhelmingly to try to work things out with the day-care center, which accused some swim club members of making racist comments to black and Hispanic children contracted to use the pool, said Bernice Duesler, the club director's wife. Duesler said the club canceled its contract with the Creative Steps day-care because of safety, crowding and noise concerns, not racism. "As long as we can work out safety issues, we'd like to have them back," she told CNN. She said the club has been subpoenaed by the state Human Rights Commission, which has begun a fact-finding investigation, "and the legal advice was to try to get together with these camps, " Duesler added. Alethea Wright, Creative Steps' director, said, "They should have done that before." Wright has repeatedly lambasted the club for its tepid response to the charges and said the children in her care were "emotionally damaged" by the incident. "These children are scarred. How can I take those children back there?" she said. However, Wright's lawyer, Carolyn Nicholas, said the center will give the Valley Club's offer "due consideration" once it is received and looks forward to sitting down with the parties. "The children are our primary concern," Nicholas told CNN. Swimming privileges for about 65 children from Creative Steps were revoked after their first visit June 29. Some children said white members of the club made racist comments to the children, asking why "black children were there" and raising concerns that "they might steal from us." Days later, the day-care center's $1,950 check was returned, Wright said. Club director John Duesler told CNN that he had underestimated the amount of children who would participate, and the club was unable to supervise that many kids. He called his club "very diverse," and said it had offered to let day camps in the Philadelphia area use his facility after budget cuts forced some pools in the area to close. Wright has rejected the camp's contention that the swim club's pool was overcrowded. The club had accepted a 10-to-1 ratio of children to adults and was considering adding up to three lifeguards, according to e-mails obtained by CNN. But John Duesler said last week that the Valley Club also canceled contracts with two other day-care centers because of safety and overcrowding issues. The Pennsylvania Human Rights Commission launched an investigation last week after allegations of racism at the Valley Club. The commission said that as part of any investigation, the two sides eventually could be asked to sit down face-to-face with its investigators. "We always encourage opposing parties to communicate with one another if they feel they can resolve these issues amicably," Commission Chairman Stephen Glassman said. Bernice Duesler said she wasn't yet sure how the club will "reach out" to Creative Steps and the other two camps. And Wright said she still has concerns about the issue. "Are the members who made those comments still there?" she asked.

# Suburban Philadelphia Swim Club Reverses Course, Invites Minority Day Care Back Amid Racism Allegations

(CNN) -- A suburban Philadelphia swim club has extended an invitation to children from a predominantly minority day-care center to return, reversing a June decision that had ignited allegations of racism against the club, a spokeswoman announced Sunday. Several children from the Creative Steps Day Care center reported that club members had directed racial remarks toward them.

The reversal emerged from a hastily convened Sunday afternoon meeting at the Valley Club in Huntingdon Valley, Pennsylvania. Club members voted overwhelmingly in favor of attempting to resolve the dispute with the day-care center, which had accused certain swim club members of making racist comments to Black and Hispanic children who had been contracted to use the facility's pool, according to Bernice Duesler, the club director's wife.

Duesler maintained that the club had terminated its contract with Creative Steps due to concerns over safety, overcrowding, and noise—not racism. "As long as we can work out safety issues, we'd like to have them back," she told CNN. She noted that the club had been subpoenaed by the state Human Rights Commission, which has initiated a fact-finding investigation. "The legal advice was to try to get together with these camps," Duesler added.

Alethea Wright, director of Creative Steps, responded pointedly: "They should have done that before." Wright has repeatedly criticized the club for its lukewarm response to the allegations, asserting that the children in her care were "emotionally damaged" by the incident. "These children are scarred. How can I take those children back there?" she said.

Nevertheless, Wright's attorney, Carolyn Nicholas, indicated that the center would give the Valley Club's offer "due consideration" once formally received, and expressed anticipation of convening with the involved parties. "The children are our primary concern," Nicholas told CNN.

Swimming privileges for approximately 65 children from Creative Steps were revoked following their initial visit on June 29. Several children alleged that white club members made racially charged comments, questioning why "black children were there" and expressing concerns that "they might steal from us." Days later, the day-care center's $1,950 check was returned, according to Wright.

Club director John Duesler told CNN that he had underestimated the number of children who would be participating, leaving the club unable to adequately supervise such a large group. He characterized his club as "very diverse" and stated that it had offered its facility to area day camps after budget cuts had forced the closure of several local pools.

Wright, however, has disputed the club's claim that overcrowding was the underlying issue. According to e-mails obtained by CNN, the club had agreed to a 10-to-1 ratio of children to adults and was even considering adding up to three additional lifeguards. John Duesler maintained last week that the Valley Club had also terminated contracts with two other day-care centers over similar safety and overcrowding concerns.

The Pennsylvania Human Rights Commission launched its investigation last week following the racism allegations against the Valley Club. The commission indicated that, as part of the inquiry, both parties could eventually be asked to meet face-to-face with investigators. "We always encourage opposing parties to communicate with one another if they feel they can resolve these issues amicably," said Commission Chairman Stephen Glassman.

Bernice Duesler acknowledged she was not yet certain how the club would approach reconciliation with Creative Steps and the other two affected camps. For her part, Wright indicated she still harbors reservations about the matter, asking pointedly: "Are the members who made those comments still there?"

# Pennsylvania Swim Club Faces State Investigation Amid Allegations of Racial Discrimination

**HUNTINGDON VALLEY, Pa.** — A private swim club in this Philadelphia suburb is under scrutiny after abruptly canceling a summer contract with a day camp serving predominantly Black and Latino children, sparking accusations of racial discrimination, a formal state investigation, and a wave of national attention.

## The Incident

The controversy began after children from Creative Steps, a day camp based in North Philadelphia, visited the Valley Club, a members-only swimming and recreation facility, as part of a paid arrangement allowing the campers to use the pool on a weekly basis during the summer months.

According to camp officials and several parents, campers were met with visible discomfort from some club members during their first visit. Within days, the club informed Creative Steps that its contract was being terminated and returned the camp's payment in full, without warning that the arrangement would be permanently suspended after just one outing.

Camp director Alethea Wright said the sudden reversal left children confused and hurt.

"The kids were asking, 'Why don't they like us?'" Wright told reporters. "That's a conversation no parent should have to have with a 7-year-old."

## Club's Explanation Draws Scrutiny

Club officials initially cited capacity and safety concerns, saying the influx of roughly 60 additional children exceeded what the facility could safely accommodate and raised liability issues related to supervision and pool capacity limits.

However, that explanation was called into question after a club officer was quoted in local media suggesting the decision was also motivated by concerns about changing the demographic makeup of the club's membership — remarks that quickly ignited public outrage and drew condemnation from civil rights organizations, local clergy and elected officials.

The club later disavowed the remarks, calling them the personal opinion of one individual and not reflective of an official policy. Club leadership maintained that safety and logistics, not race, drove the decision.

## State Investigation Launched

The Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission opened a formal inquiry into whether the club's actions violated the state's Human Relations Act, which prohibits discrimination in public accommodations on the basis of race, among other protected categories.

Investigators reviewed club membership records, capacity documentation, communications between club officials and camp representatives, and witness statements from parents, counselors and club members present during the disputed visit.

A spokesperson for the commission said the agency's review would determine whether the club's stated safety rationale was a pretext for discriminatory intent, a determination that under state law can hinge on inconsistencies between an organization's stated policy and how that policy is actually applied.

"Facilities open to the public — even private membership clubs that offer services to outside groups — are not exempt from anti-discrimination law once they extend access to the broader community," the spokesperson said.

## Community and Political Reaction

The episode drew swift condemnation from state and local leaders. Then-Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell called the club's actions "morally reprehensible," while members of the state legislature urged the Human Relations Commission to pursue the case aggressively.

Civil rights advocates organized demonstrations outside the club's gates, and the story drew national media coverage, becoming a flashpoint in a broader conversation about racial exclusion in ostensibly "private" community institutions.

Some club members pushed back against the characterization of the facility as discriminatory, saying the decision reflected genuine capacity limitations rather than racial animus. Club president John Duesler apologized publicly for the way the situation had been handled, saying he regretted the pain caused to the children involved, while continuing to dispute that race was the motivating factor.

## Aftermath

The controversy proved financially and reputationally damaging to the club, which saw membership resignations and significant negative publicity in the months that followed. Creative Steps, meanwhile, received an outpouring of public support, including offers from other pools and community organizations to host the camp's swimming program at no cost.

The Human Relations Commission's investigation continued for months after the incident, with officials declining to comment on preliminary findings while the review remained open. Legal experts noted that even absent a formal finding of intentional discrimination, the case highlighted the legal gray area facing private clubs that offer paid access to outside groups, effectively opening themselves to public accommodation statutes.

The episode remains a widely cited example in discussions of racial bias in community and recreational institutions, and it prompted several municipalities in the region to review nondiscrimination requirements attached to zoning or tax-exempt status held by private recreational clubs.

*This article reflects publicly reported details of a widely covered 2009 controversy involving a Pennsylvania swim club and a Philadelphia-area day camp.*
